paragraphs: A potion bottle is a game convention rather than a real object, and the conventions are strict: a round or teardrop flask, a cork stopper, a liquid that fills most but not all of the volume, and a colour that codes what it does. Break any of those and players stop recognising it.
The mesh is light at 7,682 polygons and 3,853 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the liquid as its own body so a refractive material can behave properly inside the glass.
At $8 it suits games and interactive media, fantasy film and television, tabletop and illustration work, motion graphics and print. On sale since 2023.

A scale rule has a triangular section for one reason: it carries six different scales on six faces, so an architect can read a drawing at any of them by rotating the rule rather than carrying six flat ones. That cross section is the entire product design.
The mesh is minimal at 962 polygons and 963 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is exactly right for an extruded profile whose detail is entirely in the printed graduations.

At $7 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits architecture and engineering visualisation, drawing office and studio interiors, stationery and technical retail renders, education material and games. On sale since 2025.

A kilo bar is cast rather than minted, which gives it a completely different surface from a small pressed bar: slightly rounded edges, a dimpled top where the metal cooled and a stamped rather than printed set of markings. That casting finish is what identifies the weight class.
The mesh is minimal at 772 polygons and 774 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits a simple form whose realism comes entirely from the gold material and the stamped relief.

At $5 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits financial and investment visualisation, banking and commodities marketing, editorial and news illustration, vault and security scenes, and games. On sale since 2025.

A conventional alarm bell is a red dome over a striker, mounted on a backbox with the wiring behind it. The dome is the resonator, and its size sets the pitch, which is why bells in large buildings look bigger rather than louder. It is one of the most recognisable safety fittings anywhere.
The mesh is light at 7,906 polygons and 3,960 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the dome, the striker and the mounting plate.

At $4 it suits building safety and fire system visualisation, commercial and institutional interiors, architectural compliance material, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2023.

The C clef is the movable one: unlike the treble and bass clefs it can sit on any line of the stave, and wherever it sits marks middle C. Its shape is two curved lobes meeting a vertical bar, and rendering it as a solid object means giving depth to a form that exists only as ink.
The mesh is minimal at 1,660 polygons and 1,626 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits a graphic form with flat faces and a clean extruded profile.

At $1 this is the least expensive asset in the catalogue, and it does what a cheap symbol should: music education and notation material, motion graphics and titles, album and concert design, app and interface illustration, and print. On sale since 2015.

Anatomical reference has historically been built from a very narrow range of body types, and a model with realistic Asian skin and features addresses a genuine gap: teaching material and patient communication work better when the figure resembles the audience. Under the skin the full system stack is present.

The mesh runs 722,171 polygons and 742,600 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is what a complete body needs if muscle bellies, vessels and nerve paths are all to read correctly at close range.

At $799 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits medical and health education, clinical and patient communication, courseware and textbook illustration, research and pharmaceutical presentation, and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2025.

A figure with both skin and anatomy lets a presentation fade from the person to the structures beneath, which is the single most useful move in medical explanation. That only works when the skin sits correctly over everything underneath rather than being modelled as a separate shell.

The texture load is extraordinary: 777 maps in total, with 3 at 8192x8192, 139 at 4096x4096, 413 at 2048x2048 and 222 at 1024x1024, on a mesh of 677,003 polygons and 679,569 vertices. That is a map per structure rather than a shared atlas.

At $599 it suits medical and health education, clinical and patient communication, courseware and textbook illustration, research and pharmaceutical presentation, and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2020.

A logistics scene needs a fleet, not a truck. Different cab styles, different trailer types and different liveries are what make a yard or a motorway look like commerce rather than like the same vehicle repeated, and every unit here arrives rigged so wheels turn and cabs steer.
Buying them as a collection also keeps the scale and the surface treatment consistent between vehicles, which is the detail that gives away a fleet assembled from separate sources.
At $599 it suits logistics and supply chain visualisation, highway and depot scenes, fleet and manufacturer marketing, film and television, and games. On sale since 2020.

Analysis and news work rarely needs one platform in isolation. A strike package involves aircraft, missiles, launch vehicles and naval units acting together, and a graphic that explains it needs all of them at a consistent scale and finish - which is exactly what a collection provides and single purchases do not.
Supplying them together also keeps the modelling standard consistent, so a wide graphic showing several systems does not have one unit that visibly came from somewhere else.

At $579 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits defence and geopolitical visualisation, news and documentary graphics, strategic analysis material, training presentation and games. On sale since 2026.

A skinless figure is the working state of anatomical reference: musculature, vasculature, nerves and organs all visible at once, with nothing over them. Female anatomy differs from male in pelvic geometry, muscle proportion and organ arrangement, and a scaled male figure will teach the wrong thing.
The mesh runs 763,741 polygons and 768,419 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which is the density a complete system stack needs if each layer is to hold up under a close camera.

At $499 it suits medical and health education, clinical and patient communication, courseware and textbook illustration, research and pharmaceutical presentation, and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2022.

This is the anatomy build without the outer skin, which is how the asset is used most of the time: every system visible, nothing obscuring the structures being discussed. The texture set is enormous at 772 maps, including one at 8192x8192, 136 at 4096x4096, 413 at 2048x2048 and 222 at 1024x1024.
The mesh runs 668,515 polygons and 671,050 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, spread across the skeletal, muscular, vascular, nervous and organ systems.

At $499 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits medical and health education, clinical communication, courseware and textbook illustration, research and pharmaceutical presentation, and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2020.

A soldier is a system of items rather than one costume: uniform, plate carrier, pouches, helmet, belt kit, pack and boots, each from a different manufacturer and each fitting over the last. Assembling that from separate purchases almost never works, because the layers were not built to sit together.
Supplying the uniform and the equipment as one collection solves exactly that: the pouches fit the carrier, the carrier fits over the uniform, and the scale is consistent throughout.

At $449 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits military and defence visualisation, film and television costume, character work for games, training material and equipment presentation. On sale since 2025.

Bone and organ together is a specific and very common teaching combination: the ribcage over the lungs and heart, the pelvis around the lower organs, the spine behind everything. Showing those two layers without muscle in between is how spatial relationships get taught most clearly.

The mesh runs 486,865 polygons and 488,161 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and the texture set runs to 646 maps including one at 8192x8192, 85 at 4096x4096, 346 at 2048x2048 and 214 at 1024x1024.

At $379 it suits medical and health education, clinical and patient communication, courseware and textbook illustration, radiology and imaging explanation, and broadcast medical work. On sale since 2020.

The shortest member of the family is an unusual aircraft to find modelled, and this build goes further by including the cabin. That combination makes it useful in ways an exterior alone is not: boarding sequences, cabin interiors, safety material and turnaround scenes all come from the same file.

It is one of the heaviest aircraft assets in the catalogue at 4,409,964 polygons and 4,567,247 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 32 texture maps at 4096x4096. That weight is the interior: seats, bins, sidewalls and galley all modelled.

Two rigged builds sit on this page at $449. The static model at $349 covers airline marketing, airport visualisation, safety and training material, film and television, and news graphics. On sale since 2017.
